To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a new magnetorheometer was designed and fabricated to characterize MRFs for high shear rates, the BP model is appropriate for characterizing MRF behavior at high shear rates, and the Mason number provides a useful physical understanding of MRFs at high shear rates.

a Searle magnetorheometer was designed and fabricated to provide a characterization tool for magnetorheological (MR) fluids at shear rates up to and above 25 000 sec-1, and the results demonstrate that the Bingham plastic (BP) constituitive model can be used to characterize the apparent viscosity of two commercial MR fluids over this entire shear range.
we have developed and characterized a magnetorheometer that successfully characterizes the rheological behavior of MRFs over the shear rate ranges of interest for MREAs.

the design and fabrication of a magnetorheometer for the characterization of high-shear-rate magnetorheological (MR) fluids and their application to the design of rotary energy absorbers.
the development of a magnetorheometer capable of measuring the rheological characteristics of MRFs at shear rates up to those encountered in MREA operation.
the characterization of the magnetorheological fluid used in the magnetorheometric rotary energy absorber (MREA).

this study has provided an experimental basis for the design of MREAs for occupant protection applications.
the Mason number provides a useful nondimensional scaling of MRFs over a wide range of shear rates and magnetic field strengths.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a magnetorheometer was developed and used to characterize the rheological properties of two MRFs at shear rates up to the shear rate range expected in MREAs.

a Searle type magnetorheometer was designed and fabricated for use at high shear rates and was successfully used to characterize the rheological behavior of MRFs over the shear rate ranges of interest to MREA design.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the Mason number provides a useful tool for understanding MRF behavior at high shear rates, and thus, can be used to design MREAs that are capable of absorbing energy at these high shear rates.

the Mason number can be used to design MREAs for a wide range of applications, including occupant protection, blast mitigation, vibration isolation, and shock mitigation, and that the Mason number provides a physical interpretation for the high-shear behavior of MRFs.
a Searle-style rheometer can be used to characterize MRF behavior at shear rates of interest for MREA applications.
